content.title: THE DEFICIENCY SIGNS {{DOCTORS}} OFTEN MISS ON A ROUTINE CHECKUP
facts: **Restless legs at night** – an overwhelming urge to move your legs while trying to sleep can point to low iron or low magnesium stores.
**Mouth ulcers** – frequent canker sores or a sore, cracked spot at the corner of your mouth can signal low iron, B12, or folate.
**White spots on nails** – small white marks appearing on your nails are often linked to low zinc.
**Brittle, ridged nails** – nails that split or develop vertical ridges easily can point to a biotin or iron shortfall.
**Muscle twitches under the eye** – an eyelid that keeps twitching on its own is a classic low-magnesium sign.
**Bleeding gums when you brush** – gums that bleed easily even with gentle brushing can signal low vitamin C.
**Unexplained bruising** – bruises that show up without a clear bump can point to low vitamin C or vitamin K.
**Pins and needles in fingers** – tingling or numbness in the hands can be an early sign of low B12.
**Hair shedding in clumps** – noticeably more hair in the shower drain than usual can be linked to low iron or zinc.
**Feeling cold when others aren't** – constantly reaching for a sweater while everyone else is comfortable can point to low iron or low iodine.
**Slow-healing cuts** – small scrapes that take forever to close can signal low zinc or low vitamin C.

content.caption:
A twitching eyelid is one of the most overlooked magnesium clues — magnesium helps regulate the signals between your nerves and muscles, so when levels drop, small involuntary spasms like that start popping up. Bleeding gums get written off as a brushing problem, but vitamin C is actually essential for building and repairing the collagen that holds your gum tissue together, so a shortage shows up there before almost anywhere else. And that restless, can't-sit-still feeling in your legs at night often traces back to iron, since iron plays a role in dopamine regulation and nerve function, both of which affect how 'settled' your legs feel. Everyone's body is different, so treat these as clues worth checking, not a diagnosis.
